questions.question: What is the difference between == and is in Python?
questions.title: == vs is in Python
questions.direct_answer: == compares values using equality rules; is compares object identity, meaning whether two names refer to the same object. Use == for values and reserve is for singleton checks such as value is None.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can avoid identity and interning surprises.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using is to compare strings or integers because small values sometimes appear interned.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the safe idiom `if value is None` and explain that identity is an implementation detail for ordinary values.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define == vs is in Python simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Value versus identity
sections.content: Equality asks whether objects represent the same value. Identity asks whether they are literally the same object in memory.

sections.title: Safe comparisons
sections.content:
```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
a == b  # True
a is b  # False
value is None  # correct singleton check
```

sections.title: Remember
items: Use is for None, True, False, and other intentional singletons.
Do not depend on interning of strings or integers.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Double equals compares values, while `is` compares identity. I use `==` for normal comparisons and `is None` for the None singleton; interning can make identity look reliable when it is not.
